value: oleic acid gave a strong repellent activity against both sexes in the laboratory ambulatory assay; hexane repelled the males
method: laboratory choice arena: wooden chamber 150 x 10 x 10 cm in fifteen sections, compound on a cotton swab at one end, distribution of walking beetles recorded on video; 50 beetles of one sex per compound per day
conditions: adults collected by Barber pitfall traps in forest around Kaunas, Lithuania, then kept in laboratory culture with sexes housed separately; 40 compounds and mixtures tested, each applied as one drop (0.05 mL) on a cotton swab with no solvent named; each compound tested once a day with 50 males or 50 females; indices are means of 22 freeze frames from one video (Table 4 'n = 22'), not independent replicate runs; no blank or solvent-control arena is described; the Results text gives no p or F values

source.authors: Faly L, Brygadyrenko V, Paulauskas A
source.title: Repellent and Attractant Activities of Organic Compounds on Female and Male Philonthus decorus (Coleoptera, Staphylinidae)

quote: A strong repellent activity against both sexes of Ph. decorus was caused by oleic acid, while hexane repelled the males.
note: Same paper, qualifying the abstract: Results say 'Hexane was a strong repellent against the males and was neutral to the females' and call oleic acid 'High repellent activity against both sexes'; the abstract also says females were in general less sensitive and that the rest of the 40 compounds caused no ambulatory response. Effects are categories of the authors' attraction-index scale (Table 3: '0.125–0.249—strong repellent activity', '0.500–1.999—absence of activity'); the index is the ratio of beetles on the four squares nearest the odour source to those on the four remotest; Methods say males and females 'were compared using ANOVA', and Table 4 (indices, n = 22, compounds ordered by significance of the sex difference) is an image on the page and was not read; the Results text prints no p or F value. Licence: the page prints no licence sentence and its metadata lists CC BY 3.0; Crossref gives CC BY 4.0, vor, start 2024-04-25 (CC BY 3.0 page versus CC BY 4.0 Crossref). Name (audit 469): baza.biomap.pl prints 'Philonthus (Philonthus) decorus (J.L.C. Gravenhorst, 1802)', 'name status: valid name', Staphylinidae, Staphylininae, Coleoptera. Chemical avoidance in a walking assay: no receptor or sense organ is identified. Licence (audit 469): page prints no licence sentence, metadata CC BY 3.0; Crossref one licence, https://creativecommons.org/licenses/by/4.0/, vor, start 2024-04-25; accepted case. value: a female responded in 65 of 120 playback tests of a synthesized male calling signal (MCaS) played back on single tea leaves
method: playback of a synthesized signal built from a pre-recorded MCaS unit (1.491 s, dominant frequency 340.8 Hz) repeated at 2.5 s intervals to a 5 min signal (Adobe Audition), played on the second, fourth, sixth, seventh, eighth and tenth leaves under the bud of 20 tea branches while a female sat on the seventh leaf; a new female for each test
conditions: test females were 'Sexually mature seven-day-old virgin' adults from 'the second and subsequent generations' reared on Longjing 43 tea branches in an insectary (L10:D14, 25 ± 2 °C, 75 ± 5% RH), founded from adults collected at the Tea Research Institute, CAAS, Hangzhou, China, September to November 2023 and 2024; each leafhopper tested once; no silence (no-playback) control is reported, so spontaneous female signalling is not separated from responses; the paper gives no explicit definition of a female response (female signals on her leaf were recorded)

source.authors: Shan Y, Yao Q, Jia Q, Lu J, Cai X, Chen Z, Bian L
source.title: The Effect of Leaf Traits on the Excitation, Transmission, and Perception of Vibrational Mating Signals in the Tea Leafhopper Empoasca onukii Matsuda (Hemiptera: Cicadellidae)

quote: A total of 65 females responded to the MCaS playback out of a total of 120 tests performed.
note: Null in the same paper: 'none of the MCaS parameters affected female responses (p > 0.05' (whether a female responded); the Results give no response frequency by playback leaf. The paper names the species Empoasca onukii; the repository's GBIF name list gives Empoasca onukii as a SYNONYM of Matsumurasca onukii, so the accepted name is used here (audit 469: species.biodiversitydata.se gives Matsumurasca onukii (Matsuda 1952) as accepted, Cicadellidae, Hemiptera, with synonyms Empoasca onukii (Metcalf 1968) and Chlorita onukii (Ishihara 1953); main's precedent desk-d236 after audit 330). Licence: the page prints no full licence sentence (metadata lists CC BY 3.0); Crossref gives CC BY 4.0, vor, start 2025-04-07. MCaS is the paper's abbreviation for the male calling signal; playback is of a synthesized signal, not of live males. Significant results in the same section, among the 65 responding tests: 'The multiple linear regression model of NFS1 was significant (F4,60 = 2.765, p = 0.035)', 'the effect of IMCaS-S0 was significant (t = 2.012, p = 0.049)'; DelayID model 'F1,63 = 4.976, p = 0.029', DMCaS-S1 't = 2.231, p = 0.029'. The null sentence ends 'which indicated that whether the female responds to the MCaS was only related to the female's physiological state'. value: the light-startle response, and habituation of it, occurs when lights are turned on and when lights are turned off
method: Experiment 1: startle response of individual cockroaches to room lights switched on or off across repeated trials, n = 96 cockroaches
conditions: adult cockroaches 'that had intact antennae and legs, and at least half of their wings' (sex not stated), from a laboratory breeding colony whose founders came from three commercial suppliers (Roach Crossing, Josh's Frogs, Cape Cod Roaches); Experiment 1 stimulus four fluorescent room lights (32 W, 2196 lumens each) with two 3 W red bulbs for illumination; a startle was 'any change in location inside the apparatus during the trial'; eight alternating light-on and light-off trials 30 min apart after 1 or 24 h acclimation with room lights on or off; light colour of the later flashlight stimulus not stated

source.title: Habituation of the Light-Startle Response of Orange Head Cockroaches (Eublaberus posticus): Effects of Acclimation, Stimulus Duration, Presence of Food, and Intertrial Interval

where: Abstract, sentence returned in two consecutive pieces and joined
quote: In our first experiment, we found that LSR, and habituation of LSR, occurs to both lights being turned on and lights being turned off.
note: LSR is the paper's abbreviation for light-startle response. Qualifiers in the same paper: Experiment 1 Results give overall response probability lower for light-on trials (estimate = -1.918, p = 0.005) and lower for subjects with a light-on acclimation period (estimate = -2.839, p < 0.000); Experiment 2 (stimulus 2, 4, 8 or 10 s, 100-lumen flashlight) found that light duration did not affect response. Whole-field light change with no wavelength or eye-specific test, so no spectral or visual-organ claim. Licence: page prints no licence sentence (metadata lists CC BY 3.0); Crossref gives CC BY 4.0, vor, start 2021-04-11. Name (audit 469): Cockroach Species File prints 'Eublaberus posticus (Erichson, 1848)', Blaberidae, Blaberinae, Blattodea, original combination Blabera postica Erichson, 1848. Further results in Experiment 1: with light-on acclimation 'the trends were less clear' and 'no clear differences were observed between light-off and light-on trials'; 'startle probability somewhat increased with weight (estimate = 0.411, p < 0.003)'; the decline across trials was significant (estimate = −3.09, p < 0.000) and similar across conditions (p values > 0.251).
